intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome (CLPED1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NECTIN1 gene (PVRL1; 600644). Heterozygosity for a NECTIN1 mutation has been associated with sporadic nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate (OFC7) in northern Venezuela.

checks.evidence_quote: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutations of the poliovirus receptor-like 1 (PVRL1) gene encoding nectin-1.
checks.explanation: The abstract says the syndrome is caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutations in PVRL1. NECTIN1 is the current approved symbol for PVRL1.

checks.explanation: The abstract reports that heterozygosity for the PVRL1 (NECTIN1) W185X mutation is associated with sporadic non-syndromic CL/P in northern Venezuela. NECTIN1 is the approved symbol for PVRL1. OFC7 is OMIM's label for this phenotype, so it counts as standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the PVRL1 gene, which encodes nectin-1 (Yoshida et al., 2015). Clinical features include unusual facies, dental anomalies, hypotrichosis, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and onychodysplasia, syndactyly, and cleft lip/cleft palate (Suzuki et al., 1998). Some patients have mental retardation (Yoshida et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Bustos et al. (1991) described 27 individuals from 7 families, related to each other with high probability, from a relatively isolated and inbred population with very small neighboring communities on Margarita Island in northeastern Venezuela (Nueva Esparta State). Affected individuals showed manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia and other anomalies with variable expressivity, and females were affected as severely as males. All parents were normal. The authors stated that the clinical picture common to all patients could not be classified within the known ectodermal dysplasias.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora et al. (1987) concluded that the syndrome in their 2 sibs was most probably inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder. Oğur and Yüksel (1988) reported affected brothers born to second-cousin parents, and Rodini and Richieri-Costa (1990) reported 3 affected brothers born to normal consanguineous parents, discussing the pattern of inheritance as autosomal recessive. Bustos et al. (1991) concluded that the disorder in the Margarita Island families, in which all parents were normal and females were affected as severely as males, was a newly recognized autosomal recessive syndrome. Suzuki et al. (2000) described CLPED1 as autosomal recessive, and Yoshida et al. (2015) found homozygosity for a PVRL1 mutation in an affected child whose parents were heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: In a 7-year-old Japanese boy, born of consanguineous parents, with CLPED1, Yoshida et al. (2015) identified a homozygous c.400C-T transition in exon 2 of the PVRL1 gene, resulting in an arg134-to-ter (R134X) substitution. His parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The mutation was predicted to result in a truncated protein lacking the transmembrane and intracellular domains of nectin-1.

checks.claim: Yoshida et al. (2015) identified a homozygous c.400C-T transition in exon 2 of the PVRL1 gene, resulting in an arg134-to-ter (R134X) substitution, in a 7-year-old Japanese boy with CLPED1.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis of exon 2 of PVRL1 revealed a novel homozygous nonsense mutation, c.400C>T (p.Arg134*).
checks.explanation: Equivalent notation; C>T is a transition.
